When it is played, the vibration of the strings is amplified by the resonating cavity of the wooden body, producing a sound that is both delicate and forceful. Its characteristic nasal quality and long-ringing aftertone give it a recognisable signature in Mongolian folk music, and it can convey both the boldness and the depth of a nomadic people.

託布秀爾具有溫暖而富有穿透力的音色，音質兼具明亮與醇厚的特徵。其音域寬廣，從低沉: The topshur has a warm timbre with good carrying power, bright and full at once. Its range is wide, with a marked span from the low fundamental to the high overtones. Because it has two or three strings, its resonance has an unusual harmonic structure that can produce a richly layered sound.
託布秀爾為弦鳴樂器，發聲體為弦，編號321.321，流傳西蒙古衛拉特地區。材質因: The topshur is a chordophone whose sounding body is its strings, no. 321.321, current in the Oirat region of western Mongolia. Materials vary because the instruments are handmade. The body, pegbox and neck are of wood; the body may be oval, spoon-shaped, spade-shaped, cup- or bowl-shaped, square or trapezoidal, and is covered with stretched animal hide or fish skin, with newborn camel hide or the hide from an animal's flank used to get a thin skin. The strings vary by tribe and may be of horsehair, horse mane or sheep gut. Traditionally there are no frets, though fretted versions also exist now. The source does not state the materials of the other parts.

Marco Polo described the Mongols playing this instrument before battle. Most are handmade, so there is no standard form, and the shape of the body and the material of the strings vary with tribe and region; traditionally there are no frets, though fretted forms appeared later. The Kalmyk type is closer to the Kazakh dombra. The source gives neither the year of origin nor a founder.

It often accompanies storytellers, singing and dancing, above all the dances of tribes such as the Altai Uriankhai, the Zakhchin and the Torgut, and it also appears in traditional narrative singing. The source names no particular composer or piece, so the examples should be these oral performances and dance line-ups; Marco Polo also described the Mongols playing an instrument of this kind before battle.

The topshur (also tovshuur) is a traditional two- or three-string plucked lute of the Oirat region of western Mongolia, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321. The body is mostly bowl-shaped, oval or spoon-shaped, supported by a wooden pegbox and neck, and the soundboard is often covered with stretched animal hide or fish skin; the strings may be of horsehair, horse mane or sheep gut, and traditionally there are no frets, though fretted versions also exist now. It is used by the Altai Uriankhai, the Altai people, the Tuvans and the Khalkha Mongols, often to accompany narrative singing, song and dance, and Marco Polo described the Mongols playing it before battle.
